title: Suthida
text:
Suthida, now Queen of Thailand, was born Suthida Tidjai on June 3, 1978. She is the fourth wife of King Vajiralongkorn. Her ancestry traces back to a Thai Chinese family of Hokkien ethnicity. She received her education at Hatyaiwittayalai Somboonkulkanya Middle School and later earned a bachelor’s degree in communication arts from Assumption University in 2000. 

Before entering royal service, Suthida worked as a flight attendant, first for JALways, a subsidiary of Japan Airlines, from 2000 to 2003, and then for Thai Airways International from 2003 until 2008. In 2014, she joined the Thai military and was appointed commander of the Crown Prince’s household guard. By 2016, media reports identified her as a consort to the then-Crown Prince, though the palace did not officially confirm this. She was promoted to the rank of general in December of that year, having rapidly risen through the ranks in just six years of service, and became Commander of the Special Operations Unit of the Royal Security Command. In 2017, she was appointed acting commander of the Royal Thai Aide-de-camp Department.

Recognition of her position came with the bestowal of the title Than Phu Ying on October 13, 2017, when she was named a Dame Grand Cross (First Class) of The Most Illustrious Order of Chula Chom Klao – the first female officer to receive this honour since 2004 and during the reign of King Rama X. 

Suthida officially became Queen of Thailand on May 1, 2019, coinciding with the coronation ceremonies for King Vajiralongkorn held in Bangkok from May 4th to 6th. The marriage registration was witnessed by Princess Maha Chakri Sirindhorn and President of the Privy Council Prem Tinsulanonda. Most recently, on May 10, 2024, she accompanied the King in presiding over the Royal Ploughing Ceremony in Bangkok. 

Alongside her title, Queen Suthida holds numerous honors and awards, including being a Dame of The Most Illustrious Order of the Royal House of Chakri and The Ancient and Auspicious Order of the Nine Gems, as well as various Grand Cordon and Medal distinctions. Her military career has seen a swift progression, holding ranks from Second Lieutenant in 2010 to General by December 2016, with further advancement to Admiral and Air Chief Marshal scheduled for March 6, 2025.

title: Miguel Ángel Félix Gallardo
text:
Miguel Ángel Félix Gallardo, known as “El Jefe de Jefes” or “The Boss of Bosses,” was a key figure in the establishment of the Guadalajara Cartel, which dominated Mexican drug trafficking in the 1980s. Born in 1946 in Sinaloa, he initially worked as a police officer and leveraged political connections – including being the godfather to a governor’s son – to build his criminal organization. He rose to prominence by brokering corruption and taking control of trafficking routes after the death of a previous trafficker.

The Guadalajara Cartel’s success stemmed from a deal with Colombian cartels, who began using Mexico as a transit point for cocaine due to increased interdiction efforts in Florida. Rather than accepting cash, Félix Gallardo’s cartel took a 50% cut of the cocaine they transported, generating an estimated $5 billion annually. By the end of the 1980s, the Guadalajara Cartel, which would later splinter into the Sinaloa, Tijuana, Juárez, and Pacifico Sur cartels, had a near monopoly on the Mexican drug trade.

Félix Gallardo’s operations came under intense scrutiny following the 1985 kidnapping and murder of DEA agent Enrique “Kiki” Camarena. Camarena had been investigating the cartel’s marijuana plantations and uncovering connections between drug traffickers, Mexican law enforcement, and government officials within the ruling PRI party. Félix Gallardo allegedly ordered Camarena’s abduction, which led to a brutal torture and murder. This sparked “Operation Leyenda,” a massive DEA investigation that ultimately implicated Félix Gallardo and his associates.

Arrested in 1989, Félix Gallardo was charged with Camarena’s murder, racketeering, and drug smuggling. Though initially protected by political influence, he was eventually convicted and sentenced to 40 years in prison, later increased to 77 years after a 2017 trial. Even while incarcerated, he maintained influence within the drug world, communicating via mobile phone. 

Critically, Félix Gallardo orchestrated the division of his organization before his ultimate loss of control. In 1989, he brought together the country’s top drug lords and designated territories to them, effectively creating the foundations for the modern cartels. This included assigning routes to his nephews, the Arellano Félix brothers (forming the Tijuana Cartel), the Carrillo Fuentes family (Juárez), Miguel Caro Quintero (Sonora), and Joaquín Guzmán Loera and Ismael Zambada García (Pacific coast, forming the Sinaloa Cartel). 

His story has been dramatized in several television series, including *Narcos: Mexico* and *El Cartel*, and he penned memoirs while in prison, detailing his life and experiences. His arrest is widely considered a turning point, exposing widespread corruption in Mexico and ultimately contributing to the escalating Mexican Drug War. He was granted house arrest in September 2022, citing declining health, a decision applauded by Mexican President Andrés Manuel López Obrador.

title: Jan Zamoyski
text:
Jan Zamoyski, born in 1542 and dying in 1605, was a pivotal figure in the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth, serving as a nobleman, magnate, statesman, and the first ordynat of Zamość. He rose through the ranks, holding prominent positions including Royal Secretary, Deputy Chancellor, Grand Chancellor of the Crown, and Great Hetman of the Crown, becoming a dominant force in the Commonwealth’s political landscape throughout his life. He was a key advisor to both Sigismund II Augustus and Stephen Báthory, but later became a major opponent of Sigismund III Vasa.

Zamoyski received a comprehensive education, starting in Poland and continuing abroad with studies at the Sorbonne, Collège de France, Strasbourg, and Padua, where he earned a doctorate in law in 1564. During his time abroad, he converted from Calvinism to Roman Catholicism. He became known for his active participation in university politics, even serving as rector of the law department, and authored a work on Roman government. Upon returning to Poland in 1565, he quickly gained favor with King Sigismund II, undertaking tasks like reorganizing the Chancellery archive and commanding royal forces.

He played a significant role in the royal elections following the extinction of the Jagiellon dynasty in 1572, advocating for a viritim election – allowing all nobles to vote – but his proposal for majority rule was unsuccessful, contributing to the future instability caused by the *liberum veto*. Zamoyski became a leader of the lesser nobility, championing reform and the preservation of the Commonwealth’s unique political system, earning him the nickname “the first tribune of nobility.” He supported Henry de Valois’s election, but faced embarrassment when the king abandoned Poland. He later actively opposed the Habsburgs and facilitated the marriage of Anna Jagiellon to Stephen Báthory.

Báthory rewarded Zamoyski with positions including Deputy Chancellor and, later, Grand Crown Chancellor, and he participated in quelling the Danzig rebellion. He married Krystyna Radziwiłł, strengthening his alliance with the powerful Radziwiłł family. He contributed significantly to the preparations for war against Muscovy, demonstrating a developing military aptitude. Despite personal tragedies, including the deaths of two wives and children, he continued to serve, eventually being appointed Grand Crown Hetman, a nomination considered technically illegal at the time. He participated in the prolonged Siege of Pskov, which, although unsuccessful in capturing the city, ultimately resulted in a favorable peace treaty for Poland. 

In later years, Zamoyski initially supported Sigismund III Vasa’s ascension but soon distanced himself due to the king’s pro-Habsburg policies. He clashed with Sigismund, even engaging in a heated exchange during a Sejm session. He fought against Tatar incursions, developed a plan for a buffer state in Moldavia, and successfully intervened in Moldavian and Wallachian affairs. He also led forces against Sweden in Livonia, while simultaneously opposing the war on the political front. 

Zamoyski amassed a considerable fortune from his vast estates and invested in economic development, including colonization and industry. He founded the city of Zamość, designed as a Renaissance “ideal city,” and established the Zamoyski Family Fee Tail, effectively creating a duchy. He founded the Zamojska Academy, the third university in Poland, and was a patron of the arts. While praised for his statesmanship and military leadership, Zamoyski was also noted for his pragmatic, sometimes self-serving, nature. He died in 1605, leaving a lasting legacy as one of the most significant figures in Polish history.

title: Fernando da Costa Novaes
text:
Fernando da Costa Novaes was a Brazilian ornithologist born on April 6, 1927, and who died on March 24, 2004. He dedicated his career to the study of birdlife in the Amazon region. He earned his doctorate in 1971 from the State University of São Paulo at Rio Claro, with his thesis focusing on the ecology of birds in a secondary growth area of the lower Amazon River, in the state of Pará.

Novaes spent much of his professional life at the Museu Paraense Emílio Goeldi in Belém, where he built up the second largest bird skin and skeleton collection in Brazil. This collection was later named in his honor, recognizing his significant contribution to the museum. His research primarily focused on defining the geographical boundaries of the Amazon’s bird fauna and clarifying complex taxonomic relationships within the region’s avian species.

In 1954, Novaes received a fellowship from the Simon Guggenheim Memorial Foundation, allowing him to conduct research at the Museum of Vertebrate Zoology at the University of California, Berkeley, under the guidance of prominent ornithologist Alden H. Miller. 

Throughout his career, Novaes was a prolific publisher, with his work detailed in obituaries written by Oren and Silva. He authored and co-authored numerous articles across a variety of scientific journals including *Acta Amazonica*, *Anais da Academia Brasileira de Ciencias*, *Ararajuba*, *Arquivos de Zoologia*, *The Auk*, *Biological Conservation*, *Boletim do Museu Nacional Zoologia*, *Boletim do Museu Paraense Emílio Goeldi*, *Bulletin of the British Ornithologists' Club*, *The Condor*, *Goeldiana zoologia*, *Papéis Avulsos de Zoologia*, *Revista Brasileira de Biologia*, *Revista Brasileira de Zoologia*, *Revista Científica*, and *Summa Brasiliensis Biologiae*. These publications covered a wide range of topics, including species descriptions, geographic variation, ecological studies, and behavioral observations of various Amazonian birds.

Novaes is also commemorated in the scientific name of the Alagoas foliage-gleaner, *Philydor novaesi*, a testament to his lasting impact on the field of ornithology. His extensive body of work continues to be a valuable resource for researchers studying the birds of the Amazon and Brazil.

title: Cheyenne Brando
text:
Tarita Cheyenne Brando was born in 1970, the daughter of actor Marlon Brando and his third wife, Tarita Teriipaia, whom he met while filming *Mutiny on the Bounty*. She was primarily raised by her mother on the island of Tahiti following her parents’ divorce in 1972. Marlon Brando largely kept Cheyenne and her brother, Tehotu, from visiting the United States, believing the fast-paced American lifestyle would be detrimental to them as Tahitians. 

Initially, Cheyenne admired her father, but this affection soured as she grew older, with her later expressing resentment for his perceived neglect during her childhood. She felt he rarely visited and showed little interest in her well-being. She abandoned her formal education and began experimenting with drugs, including LSD, PCP, marijuana, and tranquilizers, while simultaneously starting a modeling career. This career was abruptly cut short in 1989 when she was seriously injured in a car accident after being denied a visit with her father during a film shoot. The crash necessitated extensive surgery.

In 1987, Cheyenne began a relationship with Dag Drollet, whose father was a politician in French Polynesia. They became pregnant in 1989 and, at Marlon Brando’s urging, moved into his Los Angeles home to prepare for the birth of their child. Tragedy struck in May 1990 when Drollet was shot and killed by Cheyenne’s half-brother, Christian Brando. Christian claimed the shooting was accidental, stating he was acting in defense of Cheyenne after she told him Drollet was abusive. 

Cheyenne refused to testify at Christian’s trial, fleeing to Tahiti and later being declared “mentally disabled” by a French judge, rendering her unable to provide testimony. Without her account, prosecutors offered Christian a plea bargain, and he ultimately pleaded guilty to voluntary manslaughter, serving five years in prison. He later expressed doubt about Cheyenne’s claims of abuse, questioning her mental state.

Following these events, Cheyenne’s mental health sharply declined. She battled drug addiction and repeatedly sought treatment in rehabilitation facilities and psychiatric hospitals. She publicly leveled serious accusations against her father, alleging both sexual abuse and his involvement in Drollet’s death, claims he denied. Eventually, she was diagnosed with schizophrenia, became increasingly isolated, and lost custody of her son, Tuki, to her mother. Tuki was raised in Tahiti and later pursued both medical school and a modeling career.

Cheyenne Brando died by suicide on April 16, 1995, at her mother’s home in Tahiti. Her funeral was held in Tahiti, and she was buried in the Drollet family crypt. Notably, neither Marlon Brando nor Christian Brando attended her funeral.

title: Radhika Apte
text:
Radhika Apte, born on September 7, 1985, in Vellore, Tamil Nadu, is a prominent Indian film and television actress. Her parents, both doctors, were stationed in Vellore at the time of her birth, and her father later became a neurosurgeon in Pune. Apte holds a degree in Economics and Mathematics from Fergusson College, Pune, and initially experienced a liberating homeschooling period with friends. She began her acting journey in theatre, eventually moving to Mumbai before briefly returning to Pune, discouraged by her initial experiences. A year spent studying contemporary dance in London proved transformative, exposing her to a different professional environment and leading to her meeting her future husband, London-based musician Benedict Taylor, whom she married in 2012. 

Apte’s film career began with a small role in the 2005 Hindi film *Vaah! Life Ho Toh Aisi!* and gained momentum with her lead role in the 2009 Bengali drama *Antaheen*, where she was praised for her performance as a TV journalist. Throughout the early 2010s, she appeared in a variety of films across multiple languages, including Marathi, Hindi, Tamil, and Telugu, often tackling challenging roles. She faced a setback when she was deemed “too fat” for a role in a blockbuster production, an experience she later recounted.

A turning point came in 2015 with supporting roles in *Badlapur*, *Hunterrr*, and *Manjhi - The Mountain Man*, earning her wider recognition.  Her leading roles in the independent films *Phobia* and *Parched* in 2016 further cemented her critical acclaim. Apte’s career saw a significant boost with her work on Netflix, starring in the anthology film *Lust Stories*, the thriller series *Sacred Games*, and the horror mini-series *Ghoul* in 2018.  Her performance in *Lust Stories* earned her a historic nomination for an International Emmy Award, making her the first Indian actress to receive such recognition. She continued to work with Netflix on films like *Raat Akeli Hai* (2020) and *Monica, O My Darling* (2022), and appeared in the American film *A Call to Spy* (2019) as Noor Inayat Khan. More recently, her performance in *Sister Midnight* (2024) garnered a British Independent Film Award nomination.

Alongside her independent film work, Apte has also starred in commercially successful mainstream films such as the Tamil action film *Kabali* (2016), the Hindi biographical film *Pad Man* (2018), and the Hindi black comedy *Andhadhun* (2018). She is also involved in theatre, performing with Aasakta Kalamanch and in various other plays, and has participated in several short films.  

Apte is recognized in the media as a versatile and outspoken performer, often described as a “powerhouse performer” and a “poster child of OTT.” She has also been a vocal supporter of the MeToo movement in India and has spoken out against sexual harassment within the film industry.

title: Iggy Azalea
text:
Iggy Azalea, born Amethyst Amelia Kelly in Sydney, Australia in 1990, is a rapper and songwriter who achieved international success after moving to the United States at age 16. She initially gained attention through music videos for songs like “Pussy” and “Two Times” released on YouTube, leading to her debut mixtape, *Ignorant Art* in 2011, and a recording contract with T.I.’s Grand Hustle label. 

Her breakthrough came with the 2014 release of her debut studio album, *The New Classic*. This album reached the top five on charts globally and topped the Billboard Top R&B/Hip-Hop Albums chart, making her the first non-American female rapper to achieve this feat. The album featured the hit singles “Work” and “Fancy” (featuring Charli XCX), with “Fancy” receiving a Grammy nomination. Azalea further rose to prominence through a collaboration with Ariana Grande on the song "Problem," which peaked at number two on the Billboard Hot 100, immediately following “Fancy” at number one. This made her the second act in history, after The Beatles, to simultaneously hold the top two spots on the chart with debut releases. She also secured a third top ten hit with “Black Widow” featuring Rita Ora.

Following the success of *The New Classic*, Azalea encountered difficulties with her record label and personal issues that led to the cancellation of her intended second album, *Digital Distortion*. She subsequently moved to Island Records, releasing the EP *Survive the Summer* in 2018. Later disagreements led her to establish her own independent record label, Bad Dreams, through a distribution deal with Empire. This allowed her to release her second album, *In My Defense* (2019), followed by the EP *Wicked Lips* later that year, and *The End of an Era* in 2021. In 2024, she announced her retirement from music.

Azalea’s early life involved a creative upbringing; her father was a painter and comic artist, and she began rapping at age 14. Driven by a passion for hip-hop and feeling like an outsider in Australia, she moved to the US, working and saving money to pursue her musical dreams. She lived in Miami, Houston, and Atlanta before settling in Los Angeles. She initially struggled to gain acceptance, but persisted, eventually signing with Grand Hustle Records. 

Throughout her career, Azalea has earned numerous awards, including two American Music Awards, three Billboard Music Awards, an MTV Video Music Award, a People’s Choice Award, and four Teen Choice Awards, alongside four Grammy nominations. Her music videos have accrued a significant online presence, with her YouTube channel and collaborators reaching 7 billion views and 15 videos surpassing 100 million views on Vevo.

title: Mihai Eminescu
text:
Mihai Eminescu, born Mihail Eminovici in 1850 in Botoșani, Moldavia, is widely regarded as the most famous and influential Romanian poet. He was a prominent figure in the Junimea literary society and served as an editor for the newspaper *Timpul*. His poetic career began early, with his first published poem appearing when he was just sixteen. He ultimately amassed a vast written legacy, comprising 46 volumes and around 14,000 pages of manuscripts, which were gifted to the Romanian Academy after his death. His most celebrated works include *Luceafărul*, *Odă în metru antic* (Ode in Ancient Meter), and the five *Letters* (Epistles/Satires), often exploring metaphysical, mythological, and historical themes.

The question of Eminescu’s precise birthdate is somewhat complex. While he recorded 22 December 1849 in a Junimea register, and documents from his school in Cernăuți state 15 January 1850, Titu Maiorescu ultimately adopted 15 January 1850 as the correct date, based on research including church records and confirmation from the poet’s sister, Aglae Drogli, who confirmed his birth in the village of Ipotești, near Botoșani.

Eminescu’s ancestry traces back to a Romanian family from Banat, with roots in the 17th century. His paternal ancestors moved to Blaj seeking civil liberties and educational opportunities, and later to Bukovina, where his father, Gheorghe Eminovici, became a church teacher and landowner. His mother, Raluca Jurașcu, came from a noble family with Cossack ancestry. Gheorghe Eminovici rose to prominence through service to boyars, eventually receiving the title of *sluger*. 

Eminescu’s early life was spent in Botoșani and Ipotești, followed by schooling in Cernăuți. He began his literary journey in 1866 with a poem dedicated to a deceased teacher, and quickly gained recognition through publications in literary magazines like *Familia*, where editor Iosif Vulcan suggested he adopt the more Romanian-sounding name “Eminescu.” He worked with several theatrical troupes as a clerk and prompter, eventually settling in Bucharest and taking on roles as a clerk, copyist, and translator. 

He was a co-founder of the literary circle "Orient", dedicated to collecting Romanian folklore.  He pursued studies in Vienna from 1869 to 1872, attending university as an auditor, and befriended Ioan Slavici. His association with the Junimea society, and figures like Petre P. Carp and Titu Maiorescu, profoundly influenced the rest of his life. He worked as a journalist and editor for newspapers like *Albina* and *Timpul*, writing extensively on political and social issues, including Romania’s independence and the treatment of minorities. 

The final years of Eminescu’s life were marked by declining health and a personal crisis. He received treatment in Austria and Italy, and was later hospitalized in Romania diagnosed with syphilis and treated with mercury. The cause of his death in 1889 remains a point of debate, with theories ranging from mercury poisoning to complications from a head injury, though modern scholars largely support the idea of mercury poisoning as the primary cause. Despite controversies surrounding his final years, Mihai Eminescu remains a towering figure in Romanian literature, considered by many to be the founder of the modern Romanian language.

title: David Galloway (writer)
text:
David Galloway was a multifaceted American artist and academic born in Memphis, Tennessee, in 1937 and passing away in 2019. He enjoyed a long and varied career spanning over fifty-five years, working as a novelist, curator, journalist, and professor. Galloway’s education began at Harvard University, where he was influenced by figures like Leonard Bernstein and Arthur M. Schlesinger Jr., and he later married fellow student Sally Gantt.

His professional life began with work at the Albright-Knox Art Gallery before moving into teaching positions at Trinity College Dublin and the University of Sussex, alongside freelance journalism for British newspapers. He returned to the United States briefly to help establish the Museum of Contemporary Art Cleveland before accepting a position as chairman of American studies at Ruhr University Bochum in Germany in 1972, the same year his first novel, *Melody Jones*, was published to critical acclaim. 

A significant chapter in Galloway’s career involved his role as the founding curator of the Tehran Museum of Contemporary Art in 1977, commissioned by Shahbanu Farah Pahlavi. He assembled a renowned collection of Western art, featuring artists such as Dalí, Monet, Picasso, van Gogh, and Warhol, alongside Iranian artists like Parviz Tanavoli. He left Iran shortly before the Iranian Revolution, returning to his professorship in Germany.

Alongside his academic work, Galloway wrote for the *International Herald Tribune* from 1979, developing relationships with prominent artists like Pina Bausch, Keith Haring, Yoko Ono, and Andy Warhol. He published three further novels: *A Family Album*, *Lamaar Ransom: Private Eye*, and *Tamsen*. After retiring from Ruhr University in 2002, he continued curatorial work at venues including the Venice Biennale and the Moscow Museum of Modern Art, and continued writing for publications like *Art in America* and *ARTnews*. He also curated exhibitions featuring the paintings of Marilyn Manson.

Throughout his life, Galloway contributed to over a hundred books on art, design, literature, and architecture. He also purchased and renovated the Maison de Chapitre in Forcalquier, France, transforming it into a gathering place for artists and students. He was recognized for his contributions with a fellowship from the Royal Society of Arts in 1988.

title: Maja Jager
text:
Maja Buskbjerg Jager, born December 22, 1991, is a Danish recurve archer who has competed in the Olympic Games in both 2012 and 2020 (held in 2021). She achieved a major career highlight by winning the individual championship at the 2013 World Archery Championships, a feat that earned her the Danish Sports Name of the Year award that same year. Throughout her career, she has also accumulated multiple medals at the European Games and European Archery Championships.

Jager began archery at the age of eight, initially practicing in a warehouse in Tilst, facilitated by her father’s connections as a fruit grower. She later received training from Ole Gammelgaard, a former Danish Olympic archer. A pivotal moment in her career came in 2013 when she moved to Goesan, South Korea, to train under Kim Hyung-Tak, a renowned Olympic coach. This move was part of an agreement between Kim and the Danish Archery Federation, and to fulfill residency requirements, Jager pursued and completed an undergraduate degree in computer system engineering at Jungwon University. She spent five years in South Korea, finding the initial adjustment period to be the most challenging of her life, before returning to Denmark in 2018 and beginning a postgraduate program at the Technical University of Denmark in 2019.

Jager first represented Denmark on the national team at the 2009 Archery World Cup. She participated in the 2010 and 2011 European Archery Championships, achieving ninth place individually in the latter. Her Olympic debut occurred at the 2012 London Summer Olympics, where she competed in the women’s team event alongside Carina Christiansen and Louise Laursen, setting a new Danish national record in the ranking round. 

Her breakthrough came at the 2013 World Championships in Belek, Turkey. Despite a previous lack of success in international competitions, she qualified for the elimination rounds as the eighth seed and proceeded to upset top-ranked archers Ki Bo-bae and Yun Ok-hee. In a dramatic final against Xu Jing, she won by a single millimeter in a one-arrow shoot-off, claiming the world championship title. She also secured a bronze medal in the women’s team event at the same championships. This victory was credited with increasing the popularity of archery in Denmark. 

In subsequent years, Jager continued to compete, winning a silver medal in the mixed team recurve event at the 2014 European Archery Championships and another silver in the women’s individual event at the 2015 European Games. While she didn't defend her world title in 2015, she qualified for and competed in the 2020 Tokyo Olympics (held in 2021), being eliminated in the second round. She also won a bronze medal in the women’s team competition at the 2019 European Games, and was runner-up in the individual event at the 2018 European Archery Championships.

title: Braulio Lara
text:
Braulio Armando Lara Peguero was a Dominican professional baseball pitcher born on December 20, 1988, and tragically died in a car accident in his home country on April 20, 2019. His professional career began in 2008 when he signed as an international free agent with the Tampa Bay Rays, spending his initial two seasons in the Dominican Summer League where he compiled a 7-5 record and a 3.73 ERA. After a brief release and re-signing, he progressed through the Rays’ minor league system, pitching for the Princeton Rays, Bowling Green Hot Rods, and Charlotte Stone Crabs.

In 2012, Lara was selected by the Miami Marlins in the Rule 5 draft, but was quickly returned to the Rays organization. He continued to work his way up, reaching Double-A with the Montgomery Biscuits and making a single appearance for the Triple-A Durham Bulls in 2013. He spent 2014 splitting time between Durham and Montgomery, accumulating 57 strikeouts but with a 5.77 ERA.

Lara then signed a minor league contract with the San Francisco Giants in 2014, playing for both the Double-A Richmond Flying Squirrels and Triple-A Sacramento River Cats in 2015. He saw a brief improvement in his performance with Sacramento in 2016, posting a 3.90 ERA, before signing with the SK Wyverns of the Korean Baseball Organization (KBO) League in June of that year. His time in Korea was short-lived, as he struggled with a 6.70 ERA in 17 games.

Returning to the United States, Lara signed with the Washington Nationals in 2016 and spent the 2017 season with their Double-A affiliate, the Harrisburg Senators. Becoming a free agent after the season, he then ventured to the Mexican Baseball League, signing with the Sultanes de Monterrey in 2018. A trade sent him to the Generales de Durango shortly after, but his time there was brief, being released after only two games and a short 1+1⁄3 innings pitched. Throughout his career, Lara pitched at various levels, demonstrating a consistent ability to strike batters out, but often struggled with his earned run average.

title: John Atkinson Grimshaw
text:
John Atkinson Grimshaw, born in Leeds in 1836 and passing away in 1893, was a significant English Victorian artist celebrated for his atmospheric depictions of urban night scenes. Though self-taught, he developed a distinctive style heavily influenced by the Pre-Raphaelites, characterized by accurate colour, vivid detail, and realism. He initially experimented with signing his work as “JAG”, “J. A. Grimshaw”, or “John Atkinson Grimshaw” before settling on “Atkinson Grimshaw.”

Grimshaw’s artistic process was somewhat unconventional. He openly utilized tools like the camera obscura and lenses to project scenes onto his canvases, a technique that compensated for his limitations in draughtsmanship and perspective. While controversial among some contemporaries who questioned whether such methods constituted true painting, others recognized his skill in colour, lighting, and evoking emotional responses. James McNeill Whistler, a fellow artist, even conceded that Grimshaw’s moonlit paintings predated and inspired his own “nocturnes.”

Initially working as a railway clerk, Grimshaw pursued painting full-time from the age of 24, exhibiting early works of birds, fruit, and blossom. He moved several times, eventually settling in Knostrop Old Hall and establishing a second home in Scarborough, which became a frequent subject in his art. He and his son, Arthur, were members of the Leeds Photographic Society. 

Grimshaw’s paintings often featured moonlit city streets, docks in cities like London, Hull, Liverpool, and Glasgow, and interior scenes, particularly in the 1870s under the influence of artists like James Tissot. Works like *Dulce Domum* and *On Hampstead Hill* demonstrate his mastery of light and atmosphere, capturing both the visual appearance and the mood of a scene. Later in his career, he also explored historical and literary themes, referencing works by Longfellow and Tennyson, even naming his children after characters from Tennyson’s poetry.

His paintings, while depicting the contemporary world, tended to romanticize industrial scenes, focusing on beauty rather than grime. *Shipping on the Clyde*, for example, portrays Glasgow’s docks with lyricism, accurately capturing the chill and dampness of the environment. Despite a lack of surviving personal papers like letters or journals, Grimshaw’s legacy rests firmly on his evocative townscapes.  Interest in his work saw a revival in the latter half of the 20th century, culminating in a retrospective exhibition, “Atkinson Grimshaw – Painter of Moonlight,” held in Harrogate and London in 2011. Four of his children also became painters, continuing the family’s artistic tradition.

title: Richie Dorman
text:
Richie Dorman, born on June 14, 1988, is a Welshman who has transitioned from a professional football player to a sporting director role. He currently holds the position of sporting director for Burton Albion, a League One club. Dorman originates from Hawarden in Wales, and is the brother of another footballer, Andy Dorman.

His footballing career began with time in the academy system of English club Blackburn Rovers. In 2006, Dorman moved to the United States where he played for the New Hampshire Phantoms. While residing in the US, he also participated in amateur football with the Boston University Terriers. He eventually returned to Wales for two separate periods with Airbus UK. 

Dorman then ventured into Finnish football, initially joining Kraft on loan in April 2011. He later became a more established player with SJK, a club where he would achieve significant success. His performances for SJK were recognized in June 2014 when he was selected for the Veikkausliiga 'Team of the Month'. 

After his playing career concluded, Dorman remained with SJK, but in a different capacity. On October 30, 2018, he was appointed as the club’s technical director. He held this position for several years before moving back to Britain. 

In May 2023, Dorman departed SJK and took on the role of sporting director at Burton Albion. During his time with SJK as a player, the club enjoyed a period of success, winning several trophies. These included the Veikkausliiga title in 2015, the Finnish Cup in 2016, and the Finnish League Cup in 2014. Prior to their Veikkausliiga win, SJK also secured the Ykkönen title in 2012, demonstrating a climb through the Finnish football league system.

title: Katherine Ryan
text:
Katherine Ryan, born in June 1983, is a Canadian comedian, writer, presenter, actress, and singer who has built a prominent career in British entertainment. She frequently appears on popular panel shows like *8 Out of 10 Cats*, *Never Mind the Buzzcocks*, *A League of Their Own*, *Mock the Week*, *Would I Lie to You?*, *QI*, and *Have I Got News for You*. She also hosted the BBC Two show *Hair* from 2015. 

Ryan’s early life was spent in Sarnia, Ontario, with her parents, Finbar, an engineer, and Julie McCarthy, an IT consultant, and two younger sisters. Her parents separated during her teenage years. She studied city planning at Ryerson University where she began performing stand-up comedy at open mic nights, supplementing her studies with work at Hooters, where she eventually became a corporate trainer. This work brought her to the UK, initially for a month in 2007, before she moved permanently in January 2008 after her then-partner wanted to explore London. 

She began her career winning the Funny Women award in 2008, and gained television experience with appearances on Canadian show *Video on Trial* and the Channel 4 sitcom *Campus*. She’s released two Netflix stand-up specials, *Katherine Ryan: In Trouble* (2017) and *Katherine Ryan: Glitter Room* (2019), and toured with a comedy show called *Kathbum*. Beyond stand-up, Ryan has acted in television series like *Episodes* and *Badults*, and notably created, wrote, and starred in the Netflix comedy *The Duchess*, based around a single mother in London. She also had a guest role on *Murdoch Mysteries.*

Ryan has also branched into presenting, hosting *All That Glitters: Britain’s Next Jewellery Star* on BBC Two and *Ready to Mingle* on ITV2. She hosted four series of *Your Face or Mine?* with Jimmy Carr and served as a team captain on the American show *The Fix*. In 2021 she was a contestant on *The Masked Singer* as “Pigeon” and in 2025 will be a judge on *Canada’s Got Talent* and host a reunion of *The Real Housewives of London*.

Her career has not been without controversy. In 2013, she faced criticism for a joke on *Mock the Week* deemed offensive by Filipino groups, and later faced accusations of racism for comments made during an interview regarding confidence levels. 

On a personal level, Ryan has a daughter born when she was 25 and entered into a civil partnership with Bobby Kootstra, whom she initially dated as a teenager, in 2019. They have since had a son and two daughters, with a fourth child expected in 2025. She has also publicly shared her experiences with melanoma, having been diagnosed with the skin cancer twice in her twenties and again in 2025.

title: Matthew Perry
text:
Matthew Perry, born in Williamstown, Massachusetts, in 1969, was a celebrated actor recognized internationally for his role as Chandler Bing on the television sitcom *Friends* (1994-2004). He also appeared in *Ally McBeal* and earned Emmy nominations for his work in *The West Wing* and *The Ron Clark Story*. Beyond *Friends*, Perry starred in films like *Fools Rush In*, *Almost Heroes*, *The Whole Nine Yards*, and *17 Again*, and led the NBC series *Studio 60 on the Sunset Strip*. He also co-created, wrote, and starred in the short-lived ABC sitcom *Mr. Sunshine* and later co-developed and starred in a revival of *The Odd Couple*. He had recurring roles in *The Good Wife* and *The Good Fight*, and portrayed Ted Kennedy in *The Kennedys: After Camelot*. His final televised appearance was in *Friends: The Reunion* (2021), and he also lent his voice to the video game *Fallout: New Vegas*.

Perry’s early life was marked by his parents’ separation when he was one year old. He was raised primarily in Ottawa, Canada, by his mother, a journalist, and step-father, a broadcast journalist, though he also spent time in Toronto and Montreal. He attended boarding school at Ashbury College. His childhood included behavioral issues, including theft and fights, which he later attributed to feeling like an outsider. He began drinking at 14 and daily by 18. He was a promising tennis player but abandoned the sport after moving to Los Angeles at 15 to live with his actor father. He then pursued acting, studying at the Buckley School and taking improvisation classes. His early television credits include appearances in *Silver Spoons* and *Growing Pains*.

His breakthrough came with *Friends*, where he was the youngest of the main cast and earned $1 million per episode alongside his co-stars by 2002. While achieving fame, Perry privately battled severe addiction to drugs and alcohol for most of his life. He underwent numerous rehab treatments, including a stay in 2000 for pancreatitis and multiple periods of inpatient care. He struggled with Vicodin, alcohol, and other substances and admitted to having gaps in his memory during filming *Friends* due to his addiction. 

Despite his personal struggles, Perry became a vocal advocate for rehabilitation. He received the Champion of Recovery Award from the White House in 2013 and opened Perry House, a rehab center, though it later relocated. He detailed his experiences in his 2022 memoir, *Friends, Lovers, and the Big Terrible Thing*, which became a bestseller. 

Perry died on October 28, 2023, at the age of 54, from an accidental drowning caused by the acute effects of ketamine. His death was later determined to be contributed to by the effects of buprenorphine. Following his death, five individuals were charged with aiding in obtaining lethal doses of the drug. A funeral was held at Forest Lawn Memorial Park, attended by his family and *Friends* co-stars, and a foundation was established in his name to support those struggling with addiction.

title: Abdulqawi Yusuf
text:
Abdulqawi Ahmed Yusuf is a Somali lawyer and judge currently serving on the International Court of Justice (ICJ), having been appointed in 2009. He notably served as the President of the ICJ from 2018 to 2021, becoming the third African to hold the position, following judges from Nigeria and Algeria. He has announced his resignation, effective September 30, 2025, before the conclusion of his term in February 2027, prompting a future election to fill the remainder.

Born in Eyl, Puntland, Somalia, Yusuf pursued higher education in law, earning a Juris Doctor from the Somali National University and a PhD in international law from the Graduate Institute of International Studies of Geneva. He supplemented his education with post-graduate studies in international law at the University of Florence in Italy. He is proficient in five languages: Somali, Arabic, English, French, and Italian.

Prior to his role at the ICJ, Yusuf held a distinguished career in international organizations. He was the Legal Adviser and Director of the Office of International Standards and Legal Affairs for UNESCO from 2001 to 2009. Before that, he served with the United Nations Industrial Development Organization (UNIDO) in Vienna as Legal Advisor and later as Assistant Director General for African Affairs. Earlier positions include Representative and Head of the New York office of the United Nations Conference on Trade and Development (UNCTAD), and Chief of the Legal Policies Service of UNCTAD. He also lectured in law at both the Somali National University and the University of Geneva and was a delegate for Somalia at the Third United Nations Conference on the Law of the Sea.

Beyond his positions within international bodies, Yusuf is a respected scholar in the field of international law. He was elected to the Institut de droit international in 1999 and remains a member. He founded and continues to serve as the General Editor of the *African Yearbook of International Law* and is a founder and chairperson of the executive committee of the African Foundation for International Law. He has authored and edited numerous publications on international law, including books focusing on Pan-Africanism, intellectual property, and trade. He also contributes articles to newspapers concerning current affairs in Northeast Africa and Somalia. He is involved with several editorial boards and institutes dedicated to international law and relations. He previously served as a judge *ad hoc* at the ICJ.

title: Sage Stallone
text:
Sage Moonblood Stallone, born May 5, 1976, was an American actor and the eldest child of Sylvester Stallone and Sasha Czack. He had three half-sisters, Sophia, Sistine, and Scarlet Stallone, and a brother named Seargeoh “Seth” Stallone. His family also included connections to the entertainment industry through his uncle, Frank Stallone, a singer and actor, and his grandmother, Jackie Stallone. He was also the stepson of Jennifer Flavin, Sylvester Stallone’s wife.

Sage received his education at Montclair College Preparatory School in Van Nuys, California, graduating in 1993. He then spent a year studying filmmaking at the University of North Carolina School of the Arts. His initial foray into the world of entertainment came with a guest appearance on *Gorgeous Ladies of Wrestling*, a series promoted by his grandmother. 

He began his acting career appearing alongside his father in *Rocky V* in 1990, portraying Robert Balboa Jr., the son of Sylvester Stallone’s character. He repeated the experience with his father in *Daylight* in 1996, but then moved towards roles in lower-budget exploitation films. Beyond acting, Sage Stallone demonstrated an interest in film preservation. In 1996, he co-founded Grindhouse Releasing with Bob Murawski, a company focused on restoring and preserving exploitation films, including titles like *Cannibal Holocaust* and *Gone with the Pope*.

He later pursued directing and filmmaking independently. In 2006, he chose not to reprise his role in *Rocky Balboa* as he was working on *Vic*, a film he wrote, produced, and directed, which won the “Best New Filmmaker” award at the 2006 Boston Film Festival. His final acting projects involved collaborations with Vincent Gallo on *Promises Written in Water* and *The Agent*, both of which were showcased at the Venice and Toronto International Film Festivals in 2010. A childhood photograph of Sage with his father was later used in the 2015 film *Creed*, where it’s mentioned his character has moved to Vancouver. 

Sage Stallone was found dead on July 13, 2012, in Studio City, Los Angeles, at the age of 36, after not being heard from for four days. An autopsy determined the cause of death to be coronary artery disease resulting from atherosclerosis. Toxicology reports revealed only prescribed hydrocodone, given after a dental procedure, was present in his system. He was engaged to be married at the time of his death. His funeral was held at St. Martin of Tours Catholic Church in Los Angeles, and he was buried at Westwood Village Memorial Park Cemetery.

title: Namita Gokhale
text:
Namita Gokhale, born in Lucknow in 1956, is a prominent Indian author, editor, festival director, and publisher. She spent her formative years in Nainital, raised by her aunts and grandmother, and studied English Literature at Delhi University. Her life took several turns early on; she married and had two daughters while still a student, and later faced both cancer survival and the loss of her husband by the age of forty. 

Gokhale’s career began unusually with editing the film magazine *Super* at age seventeen, a role she held for seven years. She then transitioned to writing, publishing her debut novel, *Paro: Dreams of Passion*, in 1984. This novel, a satirical portrayal of Delhi’s social scene, gained both controversy and acclaim, becoming a cult classic and later re-released alongside its sequel, *Priya: In Incredible Indyaa*. While *Priya* received a more mixed reception, Gokhale continued to explore themes of societal dynamics and personal narratives in subsequent works like *Gods, Graves, and Grandmother*, which was adapted into a musical play, and *A Himalayan Love Story*. She’s also written nonfiction, including *Mountain Echoes – Reminiscences of Kumaoni Women*, which focuses on the lives of women in her ancestral region, and a version of the *Mahabharata* for children. More recently, her novel *Things to Leave Behind*, set in the Kumaon hills, has earned significant recognition, winning the 2021 Sahitya Akademi Award and appearing on the longlist for the International Dublin Literary Award.

Beyond her writing, Gokhale is deeply involved in the literary world as a facilitator and organizer. She conceptualized and hosted *Kitaabnama: Books and Beyond*, a Doordarshan show highlighting Indian literature in multiple languages. She is a founder and co-director of the renowned Jaipur Literature Festival, alongside William Dalrymple and Sanjoy K Roy, and also advises other festivals like 'Mountain Echoes' in Bhutan and The Himalayan Echo Kumaon Festival. She co-founded Yatra Books in 2005, a publishing house specializing in creative writing and translations. Earlier, she was involved with a government initiative to translate Indian literature into UNESCO languages, though funding issues led her to refocus on the Jaipur Literature Festival’s publishing imprint, Jaipur Bookmark.

Gokhale’s writing is influenced by a diverse range of authors, from Tolstoy and Dostoyevsky to Muriel Spark and Kalidasa, as well as *The Tale of Genji*. Her Kumaoni Brahmin upbringing and connection to the Himalayas are also central to her work, often exploring themes of identity and mythology. Critics have noted her “sparkling” style and acerbic wit. Throughout her career, she has received several awards, including the Centenary National Award for Literature and the Sushila Devi Literature Award, culminating in the prestigious Sahitya Akademi Award for *Things to Leave Behind*.

title: Amr Shabana
text:
Amr Shabana, born in Cairo in 1979, is a retired professional squash player widely considered one of the greatest to ever play the sport. He achieved significant success throughout his career, most notably winning the World Open championship four times – in 2003, 2005, 2007, and 2009. He also reached the World No. 1 ranking in 2006, a first for an Egyptian player. Shabana was a left-handed player who represented Egypt in team competitions, contributing to victories at the 1999 and 2009 Men's World Team Squash Championships.

His early promise was evident when he was runner-up at the British Under-14 Open in 1993, losing to Ahmed Faizy, and again at the British Under-19 Open four years later, again defeated by Faizy. He began his professional career as a PSA member in 1995, earning his first Tour title in 1999 at the Puebla Open in Mexico. He quickly followed this with a win at the Mexico Open, both times defeating Craig Rowland in the final. 

A pivotal year was 2003, where, seeded ninth, he unexpectedly won the World Open, defeating reigning champion David Palmer along the way. Following a less successful 2004, Shabana experienced a resurgence in 2005, attributing his improved form to a new coaching team and personal life changes, including marriage. This led to victories at the Heliopolis Open, St Louis Open, and Hungarian Open, culminating in a second World Open title, becoming the first player since the Khans dynasty to achieve this feat.

Shabana continued his success into 2006, winning the Canadian Classic, Tournament of Champions, and Bermuda PSA Masters, ultimately reaching the World No. 1 ranking in April of that year. He secured his third World Open title in 2007. While his reign at No. 1 ended in 2009 when fellow Egyptian Karim Darwish overtook him, Shabana continued to compete at a high level, even becoming the oldest professional to win a World Series title at the 2014 Tournament of Champions. He announced his retirement from professional squash in August 2015. Throughout his career, he amassed a total of 30 PSA titles.

title: Henryk Wieniawski
text:
Henryk Wieniawski was a Polish violinist, composer, and teacher born in Lublin in 1835 and died in Moscow in 1880. He is considered one of the greatest violinists in history, and came from a family of musicians; his brother Józef was also a notable musician, as was his nephew Adam Tadeusz Wieniawski and daughter Régine, who later published music under the name Poldowski. 

Wieniawski’s father, Tobiasz Pietruszka (born Wolf Helman), was the son of a Jewish barber who changed his name to Tadeusz Wieniawski to assimilate into Polish society and converted to Catholicism before marrying Regina Wolff, a physician’s daughter. Recognizing his prodigious talent, Wieniawski was accepted into the Paris Conservatoire at the age of eight in 1843, despite not being French, and studied there until 1846 with further study in 1849.

After graduating, Wieniawski embarked on extensive tours, frequently performing with his brother Józef on piano. He began publishing his compositions in 1847, ultimately creating a catalogue of 24 opus numbers. A significant event in his personal life was his engagement to Isabella Hampton, which was initially opposed by her parents; he composed *Légende*, Op. 17, to sway their opinion, and they eventually married in 1860. He also played viola with the Beethoven Quartet Society in London.

From 1860 to 1872, Wieniawski lived in St. Petersburg at the invitation of Anton Rubinstein, where he taught violin and led the Russian Musical Society’s orchestra and string quartet. He toured the United States with Rubinstein from 1872 to 1874, and in 1875, he succeeded Henri Vieuxtemps as a violin professor at the Conservatoire Royal de Bruxelles. 

Wieniawski’s health declined while in Brussels, forcing him to interrupt concerts. A planned Russian tour in 1879 was cut short due to illness, and he was hospitalized in Odessa. He received care from Nadezhda von Meck and benefited from a benefit concert organized by friends, but died of a heart attack in Moscow in 1880 and was buried in Warsaw’s Powązki Cemetery. His daughter, Régine, also became a composer, publishing under the pseudonym “Poldowski” after marrying an Englishman and becoming a British subject.

Wieniawski’s compositions are a cornerstone of the violin repertoire, notably his two violin concertos, the second in D minor (1862) being the more frequently performed. His *L'École moderne*, Op. 10, a set of ten etudes-caprices, is considered nearly as challenging as the famous Caprices of Paganini. He is also credited with popularizing a rigid bowing technique, sometimes called the "Wieniawski bow hold" or "Russian bow hold," which he used to achieve a distinctive "devil's staccato."  

Posthumously, Wieniawski has been honored with postage stamps in Poland (1952 & 1957) and a 100 zloty coin (1979). The first violin competition in his name was held in Warsaw in 1935, and the International Henryk Wieniawski Violin Competition has been held every five years since 1952.

title: Muhammad Al-Hafiz
text:
Muhammad Al-Hafiz, born on March 15, 1984, is a retired professional footballer from Malaysia who played as a goalkeeper. His football journey began within the youth system of Kedah FA, where he participated with the President Cup team starting in 2002. Although involved with the senior squad from 2002, his official debut didn't occur until 2004, stepping in to replace Megat Amir Faisal Al Khalidi Ibrahim. This opportunity arose due to a serious back injury sustained by Megat Amir Faisal during pre-season training.

The year 2004 was significant as it marked the introduction of the Malaysia Super League, and Al-Hafiz initially served as a second-choice goalkeeper under coach Mirandinha. However, the injury to the starting goalkeeper allowed him to make his league debut against Selangor Public Bank FC on February 14, 2004. 

Following his time with Kedah FA, Al-Hafiz moved to USM FC in the 2012 season, competing in the Premier League. His stint with USM FC was relatively short-lived, as he transitioned to Johor Darul Takzim F.C. in 2013. This move was prompted by financial troubles within the USM FC management, leading to their withdrawal from the Malaysia Premier League.

At Johor Darul Takzim, Al-Hafiz experienced greater success. Though his start to the 2013 season was somewhat inconsistent, he eventually established himself as the first-choice goalkeeper for the remainder of the year.  He became a key player for a team known for its strong roster of players.

Throughout his career, particularly with Johor Darul Takzim, Al-Hafiz accumulated several honours. He was part of the team that won the Malaysian Charity Shield in 2015. More notably, he contributed to Johor Darul Takzim securing the Malaysia Super League title in both 2014 and 2015. The team also reached the finals of other major tournaments during his time there, finishing as runners-up in the 2014 Malaysia Cup and the 2013 Malaysia FA Cup. Information regarding his career beyond these periods is not detailed in the provided article.

title: Jan-Michael Gambill
text:
Jan-Michael Gambill, born June 3, 1977, is a former American professional tennis player who reached a career-high ranking of world No. 14 in 2001. He is particularly remembered for his distinctive double-handed forehand. He began his professional career in 1996 and achieved significant results, including reaching the quarterfinals of Wimbledon in 2000 and the final of the Miami Masters in 2001. Over the course of his career, he secured three singles titles.

Growing up in the countryside of Spokane, Washington, Gambill currently splits his time between Los Angeles and Kailua-Kona, Hawaii, where he lives with his partner, Malek Alqadi, an architect and developer. He has had sponsorship deals with both Jaguar cars and Prince sporting goods. Beyond tennis, Gambill is dedicated to wildlife conservation, supporting Cat Tales Zoological Park and fundraising for Sir Elton John’s AIDS Foundation.

Gambill was inspired by tennis greats Jimmy Connors and John McEnroe as a young player, starting tennis at the age of five. He distinguished himself by defeating several highly ranked players throughout his career, including former World No. 1s like Roger Federer, Carlos Moyá, Lleyton Hewitt, Gustavo Kuerten, Marcelo Ríos, Pete Sampras, and Andre Agassi, alongside Grand Slam champions such as Michael Chang and Thomas Johansson. His most notable Grand Slam run was at Wimbledon in 2000, where he defeated Hewitt, Santoro, Goldstein and Enqvist before being stopped by Pete Sampras in the quarterfinals. He also reached the fourth round of the US Open in 2002.

A significant portion of Gambill’s career was affected by injuries. He struggled with a recurring shin condition while ranked in the top 40, which limited his play after 2004. Attempting to compensate for reduced mobility, he increased his serve speed, which ultimately led to a shoulder injury. 

After officially retiring from consistent tour play, Gambill remained involved in tennis, playing for the Boston Lobsters in World Team Tennis starting in 2008, alongside players like Agassi, Isner, and Ginepri. He briefly returned to competition in 2009 and 2010, reaching the semifinals of a Futures tournament and the quarterfinals of another. However, he has not competed on the pro tour since October 2010. He transitioned into coaching, working with CoCo Vandeweghe, a former Lobsters teammate, starting in 2011. Later, in 2017, he coached Jared Donaldson. Currently, as of 2020, he works as a sports analyst for the Tennis Channel. Gambill is openly gay and maintains a relationship with Malek Alqadi.

title: Tracy Somerset, Duchess of Beaufort
text:
Tracy Somerset, Duchess of Beaufort, born Tracy Louise Ward in 1958, is a British duchess with a diverse background as an environmental activist and former actress. She is widely known as Tracy Worcester, a name she used throughout much of her career. She descends from a prominent family; her great-grandfather was the 2nd Earl of Dudley, a Lord Lieutenant of Ireland and Governor-General of Australia who held vast land and industrial holdings. Her father was involved in the family brick business, and she is the sister of actress Rachel Ward.

Tracy Worcester began her career with modeling in Paris, followed by work at Christie’s in London and art galleries in New York. She then pursued acting, training at both the Academy of Live and Recorded Arts and the London Drama School. Her most recognized acting role was as Tessa Robinson in the television series *C.A.T.S. Eyes*, and she also appeared in *Doctor Who* and the film *Dance with a Stranger*. She also played the first Miss Scarlett in the television drama game show *Cluedo*. 

In 1987, she married Henry, Marquess of Worcester (later the 12th Duke of Beaufort), and the wedding was attended by the then Prince and Princess of Wales. They divorced in 2018, shortly after her husband inherited the dukedom. They have three children, including the current Marquess of Worcester. 

Since 1989, Worcester has dedicated herself to environmental activism. She has held trustee and directorial positions with organizations such as Friends of the Earth, The Gaia Foundation, and Farms Not Factories – an organization she founded to promote high-welfare, locally sourced meat. Her activism extends to documentary filmmaking, including *Pig Business*, which exposed the issues with intensive pig farming, and *Is Small Still Beautiful in India* and *The Politics of Happiness in Bhutan*. She actively lobbies governments and corporations, even purchasing shares in companies like Tesco to raise concerns about factory farming practices, and has undertaken undercover investigations of pig farms. 

Beyond food systems, she has been involved in broader political activism, supporting the Referendum Party, Caroline Lucas of the Green Party, and Jeremy Corbyn. She also provided bail sureties for Julian Assange. More recently, she has supported George Galloway. In 2020, she launched Forbidden Fruit and Veg, an organic market garden venture on her Badminton estate, utilizing WWOOF participants for labor and training. She also publishes a monthly newsletter dedicated to her work and causes.

title: Josh Mansour
text:
Josh Mansour, born in Sydney in 1990, is a former professional rugby league footballer of Lebanese and Cuban descent through his father, and Portuguese descent through his mother. He represented both Lebanon and Australia internationally, playing as a winger throughout his career. He began his junior career with St Johns Eagles and Kingsgrove Colts, attending Holy Spirit College in Lakemba.

Mansour’s professional journey started with the South Sydney Rabbitohs, where he played in their NYC team from 2008 to 2010, earning Winger of the Year and NYC Player of the Year accolades in 2010. He also represented Lebanon in the 2009 European Cup and the Junior Kangaroos in 2010. He progressed to South Sydney’s full-time squad in 2011, playing for their feeder team, North Sydney Bears. 

A move to the Penrith Panthers followed in 2012, after being noticed by Phil Gould. He debuted for Penrith in Round 9, scoring a try, and was named the Panthers’ rookie of the year. Over the next few years with the Panthers, he consistently improved, becoming their leading try-scorer in 2014 with 15 tries. He also received representative honours, playing for the Prime Minister’s XIII and making his debut for the Australian national team in the Four Nations tournament in 2014, scoring his first international try against Samoa.

Mansour’s career continued to climb in 2016, earning selection for New South Wales in the State of Origin series, playing in all three matches. He was also awarded the NRL’s Winger of the Year. A serious knee injury suffered during a training mishap in November 2016 sidelined him for a significant period, impacting his participation in the Four Nations tournament and the start of the 2017 season. He returned to the field in 2017, reaching his 100th NRL game and being selected for the Australian World Cup squad, although he didn’t feature in the final.

After a facial injury in 2018, requiring surgery, Mansour signed a contract extension with Penrith. In 2020, he played a key role in Penrith’s success, scoring 12 tries and reaching the NRL Grand Final, where they were ultimately defeated. Following the Grand Final, he was informed he wasn’t required for the 2021 season and subsequently signed with the South Sydney Rabbitohs. 

He spent two seasons with Souths, experiencing a knee injury in 2021 that ended his season prematurely and limited his game time in 2022. He played for Newtown in 2023 before announcing his retirement in November of that year. In early 2024, Mansour publicly voiced criticism of his former South Sydney coach, Jason Demetriou, detailing a fractured relationship and alleging dishonest communication. Throughout his career, Mansour balanced football with family life, welcoming two children with his wife, Daniella, and establishing a podcast and YouTube show called “Let’s Trot Show”. He is also a supporter of Arsenal F.C.

title: Heinrich Himmler
text:
Heinrich Himmler was a leading figure in Nazi Germany, rising to become the 4th Reichsführer of the Schutzstaffel (SS) and a key architect of the Holocaust. Born in Munich in 1900 to a conservative middle-class family, he served in a reserve battalion during World War I but didn’t see combat. He joined the Nazi Party in 1923 and the SS in 1925, steadily climbing the ranks to become Reichsführer-SS by 1929. Under his leadership, the SS expanded from a small unit to a powerful institution within the Nazi regime, known for its organizational skills and competent leadership, exemplified by figures like Reinhard Heydrich.

Throughout his career, Himmler accumulated significant power. From 1943, he headed both the Kriminalpolizei (Criminal Police) and served as Minister of the Interior, granting him control over all internal and external security forces, including the Gestapo. He also commanded the Waffen-SS, a combat branch of the SS that fought alongside the regular German army during World War II.  His role as the principal enforcer of Nazi racial policies led to the operation of concentration and extermination camps and the formation of the Einsatzgruppen death squads. He was centrally responsible for the genocide of approximately 5.5–6 million Jews, as well as the deaths of millions of others during the Holocaust.  He commissioned and oversaw the implementation of Generalplan Ost, a plan for the ethnic cleansing of Eastern Europe, resulting in an estimated 14 million deaths.

Early in his life, Himmler was a studious, though somewhat awkward, youth who struggled with his health. He kept a diary from age ten documenting his interests in current events and religion. He attempted a military career, but his efforts were thwarted by the war’s end before he could become an officer. He later studied agriculture but was drawn to nationalist and antisemitic ideologies.  He initially joined Ernst Röhm’s group and became increasingly focused on “the Jewish question”, reading antisemitic literature and participating in demonstrations. 

His involvement in the failed Beer Hall Putsch led to job loss and hardship, fueling his political radicalization. He abandoned Catholicism, embracing Germanic mythology and occult beliefs.  He joined the SS in 1925 and steadily gained influence, leveraging the party’s disarray after Hitler’s arrest to solidify his position. He developed a bureaucratic system focused on control and racial purity.  He persuaded Hitler to establish the SS as an independent organization, and under his leadership, it grew rapidly, enforcing strict racial requirements for membership. 

As the Nazi Party rose to power, Himmler’s influence expanded. He was elected to the Reichstag in 1930 and used his positions to consolidate SS control over the police and implement racial policies. He established departments like the RuSHA, dedicated to enforcing racial “purity” within the SS, and appointed key subordinates like Heydrich to build the SS’s intelligence and security apparatus. In the final years of the war, Hitler appointed Himmler to oversee the Replacement Army and the administration of the Third Reich, though he was later relieved of these commands after failing to achieve his objectives. Ultimately, he attempted to negotiate a separate peace with the Western Allies against Hitler’s wishes, leading to his dismissal, arrest, and eventual suicide while in British custody in 1945.

title: Carlos P. Romulo
text:
Carlos P. Romulo was a remarkably versatile figure in 20th-century Philippine and international affairs, serving as a diplomat, statesman, soldier, journalist, author, and educator. Born in Manila in 1899, his early life was shaped by the transition from Spanish to American colonial rule; his father initially fought against the United States but later served in the U.S. government in the Philippines. Romulo himself rose to prominence quickly, becoming a professor of English at the University of the Philippines and secretary to Senate President Manuel Quezon in the 1920s. He also became involved in publishing, serving as editor of *The Philippines Herald* and co-founding the Boy Scouts of the Philippines.

During World War II, Romulo played a pivotal role, serving as an aide to General Douglas MacArthur and actively participating in propaganda efforts after the fall of the Philippines. He became Secretary of Information in President Quezon’s War Cabinet and achieved the rank of general by the war’s end. A staunch advocate for Philippine independence, Romulo viewed American colonialism more favorably than European imperialism.

Following the war, Romulo embarked on a long and distinguished diplomatic career, serving eight Philippine presidents in various capacities. He was the country’s representative to the United States and the United Nations, and served as resident commissioner to the U.S. House of Representatives from 1944-1946 – uniquely, he was the only member to leave Congress due to his country’s secession.  At the UN, he championed human rights, freedom, and decolonization, famously responding to a belittling remark from a Soviet delegate with a spirited defense of smaller nations’ right to be heard. He served as president of the UN General Assembly from 1949 to 1950, the first Asian to hold the position, and presided over the Security Council multiple times. He was even a nominee for UN Secretary-General in 1953, but was ultimately unsuccessful.

Romulo’s commitment to the Philippines also led him back to domestic politics. He ran for the presidential nomination in 1952 but was sidelined by party politics, and later became a campaign manager for Ramon Magsaysay, who won the presidency in 1953. He held multiple cabinet positions, including Secretary of Foreign Affairs under several presidents, and Secretary of Education. He participated in the Bandung Conference in 1955, though his views on communism differed from other attendees. 

He eventually resigned from the Marcos cabinet in 1983, citing health reasons, but also expressing dismay over the assassination of Benigno Aquino.  A prolific writer, Romulo authored 22 books, including autobiographies and wartime memoirs, and was named a National Artist for Literature in 1982. He received an extraordinary number of honors and awards, including the Pulitzer Prize in 1942, and was widely respected as a leading statesman. Carlos P. Romulo died in 1985 and is remembered as a key figure in Philippine history and a significant voice on the world stage.

title: John Morris (curler)
text:
John Morris, nicknamed "Johnny Mo," is a Canadian curler born in 1978 in Canmore, Alberta, and a two-time Olympic gold medallist. He began curling at the age of five at the Navy Curling Club in Gloucester, Ontario, and his early career was marked by significant junior success. He skipped his Ottawa team to three consecutive Ontario provincial junior Men's titles from 1997 to 1999, culminating in victories at the 1998 and 1999 Canadian and World Junior Championships, where he established records for wins by a skip. 

Morris transitioned to men’s curling, initially competing out of Southwestern Ontario after attending Wilfrid Laurier University. He achieved provincial success, winning the 2002 Ontario championship and qualifying for the Brier, though he didn’t secure a national title at that time. He gained national attention at the 2001 Canadian Olympic Curling Trials, experiencing a difficult loss, and later competed in the 2003 Canada Cup, losing to Randy Ferbey. 

A pivotal move to Calgary in 2003 led to a new team with Kevin Koe, Marc Kennedy, and Paul Moffatt. While they achieved some tour success, including winning the 2004 Players’ Championship, they didn’t reach the provincial level. In 2006, Morris joined forces with Kevin Martin, embarking on a four-year plan to win Olympic gold. This partnership proved remarkably successful, with the team dominating the tour, including winning three Grand Slam events in their first season together. 

The Martin team achieved its ultimate goal at the 2010 Winter Olympics in Vancouver, winning the gold medal. They continued to excel, winning the 2008 Brier, the 2008 World Men's Curling Championship, and further provincial and Grand Slam titles. Morris was named MVP of the 2008 Brier finals. After parting ways with Martin in 2013, Morris joined Jim Cotter’s team, skipping them to a runner-up finish at the 2014 Brier. He notably became one of few curlers to represent three different provinces at the Brier, having previously played for Ontario and Alberta.

Morris then skipped a Team Canada comprised of former Kevin Koe teammates, winning the 2015 Brier and earning a bronze medal at the World Championships. He continued to switch teams and formats, eventually teaming up with Kaitlyn Lawes to win gold in mixed doubles at the 2018 Winter Olympics in Pyeongchang. Following this, he continued to compete in mixed doubles and rejoined Kevin Koe’s team as second in 2020, competing at the 2020 Brier. Throughout his career, Morris has also authored a book on curling fitness, “Fit to Curl,” and is the son of Maureen and Earle Morris, the inventor of the “Stabilizer” curling broom.

title: Arthur Ewert
text:
Arthur Ewert was a German communist activist who dedicated his life to the Communist International (Comintern), serving as a representative in several countries including the United States, China, Argentina, and Brazil. Born in 1890 in East Prussia to a peasant family, Ewert received limited formal education but was self-taught. He left rural life at 14 to become an apprentice in Berlin, later finding work in a steel factory where harsh conditions and the influence of his socialist sister radicalized him, leading to his joining the Social Democratic Party of Germany in 1908. 

He formed a long-term partnership with Elise Saborovsky, known as “Szabo,” a fellow Marxist. In 1914, they emigrated to Canada, where they became involved in the socialist movement and joined the Socialist Party of North America. When Canada entered World War I, they went underground to avoid internment, using aliases and false documents. They were eventually discovered in 1919; Ewert was deported to Germany while Szabo was interned before also being deported. 

Upon returning to Germany, Ewert joined the Communist Party of Germany (KPD) and became a key figure in preparing for a revolutionary overthrow of the government. He worked as a laborer and activist, becoming involved in street fighting and paramilitary organizing. He rose through the ranks of the KPD, becoming a member of the National Committee and Politburo in 1923. However, internal party divisions led to his removal from leadership in 1924 and reassignment to work within the Comintern in Moscow. He briefly regained his prominence within the KPD before again falling from favor in 1929 due to his association with the “Conciliator” faction.

Despite this setback, Ewert continued to work for the Comintern, utilizing his English language skills. He was sent on missions to the United States and then to Argentina in 1930, and later to China in 1932. In 1934, he and Szabo were assigned to Brazil as Comintern representatives. There, they successfully recruited Luís Carlos Prestes, a prominent Brazilian political leader, to the communist cause. 

However, their work in Brazil ended tragically. Following an unsuccessful insurrection in 1935, Ewert was arrested and brutally tortured in an attempt to reveal Prestes’s location. Both he and Szabo endured severe abuse, yet remained silent. Szabo was deported to Nazi Germany and died in a concentration camp in 1939. Ewert, mentally broken by the torture, was sentenced to a lengthy prison term.

He was released in 1945 and repatriated to East Germany, but his psychological trauma remained, and he spent the rest of his life in psychiatric care. Arthur Ewert died in 1959, and was posthumously honored by the East German government with a commemorative postage stamp in 1981.

title: Ivan Toms
text:
Ivan Toms was a South African physician renowned for his activism against apartheid and his dedication to public health. Born in Johannesburg in 1952, he received his medical degree from the University of Cape Town in 1976, following an early experience with police brutality during a demonstration against the Bantu Education system. After completing his internship, he also obtained a BA in theology.

In 1978, Toms was drafted into the South African Defence Force as a non-combatant doctor, serving in what was then South West Africa (Namibia). However, witnessing the violence inflicted on the Crossroads squatter settlement near Cape Town in 1983, where he was the sole physician for approximately 60,000 residents, solidified his opposition to the regime. This experience led him to co-found the End Conscription Campaign (ECC) in 1983, alongside activists like Nan Cross, and to refuse further service in the SADF. 

Toms actively protested government policies, notably undertaking a three-week hunger strike in 1985 to oppose the planned demolition of the Crossroads settlement. He publicly stated his moral objection to the SADF, citing his Christian beliefs. His defiance resulted in a 21-month prison sentence in 1988, though he ultimately served nine months. 

Beyond his anti-apartheid work, Toms was a pioneer in gay rights activism, becoming a founding member of Lesbians and Gays Against Oppression (LAGO) in 1987, and facing homophobic attacks as a result.  

Following the end of apartheid in 1991, Toms dedicated himself to public health initiatives. He became the national co-ordinator of the National Progressive Primary Healthcare Network, focusing on programs to combat the emerging AIDS epidemic and advocating for the use of antiretroviral drugs. He later directed the Students' Health and Welfare Centres Organisation, running mobile clinics in impoverished areas. In 1996, he assumed the role of Health Director for the City of Cape Town, later becoming the executive director of the health department in 2002.

His contributions were recognized with the bronze Order of the Baobab in 2006, awarded by President Thabo Mbeki. Ivan Toms died unexpectedly in 2008 at the age of 55 from meningococcal meningitis, and was remembered as a selfless and dedicated public servant by prominent figures such as Archbishop Desmond Tutu and the Mayor of Cape Town, Helen Zille. A centre for men's health in Greenpoint, Cape Town, bears his name, continuing his work in addressing public health challenges.

title: Kubota Beisen
text:
Kubota Beisen was a Japanese artist active during the Meiji period, born in 1852 and passing away in 1906. He distinguished himself by successfully blending traditional Japanese artistic styles with Western techniques, particularly those relating to perspective, a skill he developed independently. Beisen received his initial artistic training under Suzuki Hyakunen.

A significant part of his career involved education; he was a founding teacher at the Kyoto Prefectural School of Painting in 1878, collaborating with artist Kōno Bairei. His talent was recognized by the Imperial court in 1886 when he was commissioned to decorate the ceiling and doors of a newly constructed room within the Imperial Palace in Tokyo. In 1889, he traveled to Paris to study the works of European masters, and was subsequently awarded a Gold Medal at the Paris Exposition.

Beisen also worked as a journalist and war artist. He began working for the *Kokumin Shimbun* newspaper in 1890 and, during the First Sino-Japanese War (1894-1895), he served as a war artist for the same publication. His detailed illustrations of battlefield scenes were widely circulated, providing a visual chronicle of the conflict for the Japanese public. He was even summoned to General Headquarters to create drawings in the presence of the Emperor upon his return from the front lines.
